proof_summary: For a bound $N$, choose $M\ge N+2$ and apply the hypothesis to $n=(M+1)!/6$, obtaining primes with $(M+1)!=(6x-1)+(6(n-x)+1)$. If the Sophie Germain prime $6x-1$ were at most $N$, it would divide the factorial and hence the complementary prime, forcing an impossible equality modulo $6$; similarly, if the lower twin prime were at most $N$, its upper partner would divide the factorial and hence $6x-1$, again forcing an impossible equality modulo $6$.
